node.label: Jack Goody
node.date_label: 1963 With Ian Watt, The Consequences of Literacy · 1983 The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe · 2006 The Theft of History
node.description: Jack Goody brought anthropological comparison to histories of kinship, literacy and Eurasian societies. His jointly authored work with Ian Watt examined literacy; The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe questioned claims about uniquely European family patterns while distinguishing kinship from demographic measures. The Theft of History criticizes accounts that make European experience the template for universal historical development. His comparisons seek similarities and differences across societies; they do not establish a single timeless family system or an undifferentiated East.

sources.citation: Jack Goody, The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe (1983),8–9.

verification.note: Publisher preview imprint confirms1983. Read primary8–9 including note1, plus transition into10; not entire chapter or book. Goody explicitly questions geographic/hierarchical uniformity and uniqueness through Tibet and Roman Egypt, while distinguishing his kinship questions from demographic measures. His cited Hopkins/Carrasco studies and medieval Razi/Smith disagreement not independently checked. The criticism does not establish a contrary universal pattern or validate his whole church/property thesis. Addendum 2026-10-25: Additional 1.188 review: reread printed 8–9, including note 1, from the publisher preview. The scope remains distinctions between kinship and demographic questions, regional and social variation, and a qualified challenge to uniqueness. Cited empirical studies were not independently checked; the entire book remains unread.

verification.note: Added primary OCR101–107 and selected conclusion130–135. Two-page spreads interleave, numerical tables not visually collated; no table accuracy or whole-essay claim. Platform title/summary ignored. Hajnal103 acknowledges intermediate cases and southern variation;105 questions cross-cultural marriage definitions;107 notes urban migration;134 distinguishes existence from explanation and questions inference from isolated groups. His uniqueness and economic-mechanism claims remain attributed and contestable. Conclusion includes hypotheses in both causal directions, not proof that marriage patterns caused growth. Rest108–129 and appendix not fully read; no original-record audit. Prior metadata/de Vries check retained in history. Goody1983 criticism separately scoped.
